newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian police chief killed in NATO clash.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian police chief killed in NATO clash.

text.p: NATO-led peacekeepers on Thursday shot dead Bosnian Serb police chief Simo Drljaca who led brutal ethnic cleansing operations against Moslems and Croats in northern Bosnian in 1992.
Bosnian Serb television said he was killed during a clash in a restaurant in the town of Prijedor with peacekeepers trying to arrest him on war crimes charges. A British soldier was slightly wounded.
The report said a companion, possibly his bodyguard, died with him but this was not confirmed by British officials in London who reported Drljaca's death.
Prijedor hospital director Milan Kovacevic was arrested during the same operation on charges of complicity in genocide against Bosnian Moslems and Croats, the British said.

A Western official said Drljaca and Kovacevic were both the subject of sealed indictments issued by the U.N. war crimes tribunal in the Netherlands and were not officially aware they were liable to arrest.
The former Serb mayor of the Croatian town of Vukovar was seized last month under similar circumstances and is now in jail in The Hague where the court sits.

British NATO troops are responsible for the Prijedor sector of northern Bosnia where thousands of Moslems and Croats were driven from their homes by Drljaca's paramilitary units at the start of the war.
The region was also notorious for detention camps such as Omarska and Kereteram where Moslem and Croat men rounded up by Drljaca's force's were beaten and tortured and some killed.
NATO spokesmen at peacekeeping headquarters in Sarajevo refused to give details of the sweep against war crimes suspects in Prijedor.
Their silence fuelled rumours that the operation was continuing and that other arrests were possible during the day.
The operation gave teeth to recent warnings by the U.S.-led allies who underwrote the Bosnian peace agreement that they were ready to get tougher with scores war crimes suspects still at liberty.
The most prominent among them are former Bosnian Serb President Radovan Karadzic and his wartime army commander General Ratko Mladic who have both been indicted twice.
Mladic was seen walking openly in a central Belgrade shopping parade on Wednesday and attention has been focused again on Karadzic by his attempts to topple his successor, President Biljana Plavsic.
Plavsic, who fears she may have been compromised in Serb eyes by Western support for her during her battle with Karadzic and his hardliners condemned Drljaca's killing.

She demanded Kovacevic's release and told peacekeeping commander General William Crouch in a letter that "I fear the reaction of the people will be terrible and I cannot bear any responsibility for this."
The Bosnian Serb news agency SRNA said Drljaca was the first victim on a secret NATO list to liquidate 40 prominent Serbs but did not give other names.
An eyewitness of Drljaca's killing told Bosnian Serb police that he was confronted in a fish restaurant near Prijedor.

The incident caused tension in the town which is on the frontline with the Moslem-Croat federation in Bosnian and almost fell to enemy forces in 1995 duringn the last stages of the war when the Serb military were on the run.
One reason for the reticence of peacekeeping officials on the ground in giving details of the operation was the safety of their staff on the ground in Bosnian Serb territory.
There are around 100 staff of the Organisation of Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) in the Bosnian Serb republic and hundreds of international police.
Drljaca was sacked as Prijedor police chief last autumn at the insistence of NATO after he and his men threatened a unit of Czech peacekeepers with banned weapons.
But he was suspected of continuing to be active behind the scenes and of organising the obstruction of efforts to implement the peace process including the return of refugees.
A burly hardliner, he used to boast to journalists at Prijedor police station of his exploits in the early months of the war when a reign of terror gripped northern Bosnia.
Moslem families cowered in their homes as their menfolk were seized by armed Serb patrols in the streets of Prijedor and surrounding towns and villages.
The scenes of emaciated prisoners held behind barbed wire at Omarska shocked the world.

Drljaca claimed he was defending the West against Moslem fundamentalism and told one Reuter journalist: "What Europe has done is to cunningly put Serbs again in the position of defending it. See what a whore Europe is."
He brushed aside international condemnation saying: "There's no more messing about, we're digging in."
A Western diplomat said after learning of his death: "He's still going to stand trial but it'll be in a different court."
